utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Mark Harmon, Dan Saxon, and soon to join us Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to all the participants in the proceedings. Mr. Perisic is being represented today by Novak Lukic, Gregor Guy-Smith, and our collaborator Mr. Boris Zorko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Good afternoon, Mr. Simic, I hope you had a restful night last night.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you. Yes, I did have a good night's rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just to remind you, Mr. Simic, that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is very clear to me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you stand up, Mr. Lukic, thank you so much, Mr. Registrar, just for the record to show that the Chamber is still sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis in the absence of Judge Picard. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, once more let me say good afternoon to you personally.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will continue today, and we'll address a new topic upon which I will dwell for some time, and that topic is the operative centre of the General Staff of the VJ. While we were dealing with the general issues, you mentioned the operative centre in connection with the first administration, and we showed what that centre is. Let me now be more specific. How was the operative centre organised? You said that there were duty shifts around-the-clock. How did that function exactly?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operative centre of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia is one of the organisational units of the first administration of the sector for operations and staff affairs. It consisted of 15 persons, 13 of which were colonels, and there were two civilians there as well. Duty services organised in shifts. Three persons per shift and each shift is headed by a shift leader, so that is four shifts. Four times three, 12, and the chief of the centre is number 13. The basic function of the operations centre of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia is to have round-the-clock duty availing itself of technical resources in the field of communications, thereby gathering information through reports from units that are their immediate subordinates, or rather, units that are subordinated directly to the Chief of General Staff. Also, there is a communications system linking it to the other organs of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, such as the ministry, the customs office, the Ministry of the Interior. Information is gathered from them as well, and then all of that is assessed, processed, and on that basis a report is compiled for the preceding 24 hours. The period involved was from 0600 hours on the previous day up until 0600 hours on the present day. It involved all events that occurred in the territory, in the water space, and in the air-space and that affect the security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put a question to you, or rather, two questions on the basis of what you said just now. Let's deal with the first one. Why was it necessary for persons, officers, who work in that centre to hold the rank of colonel?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such high-ranking officers - and as I said yesterday these were persons who had spent 15 to 20 years in command positions and operative position in units at the rank of regiment, brigade, corps, respectively - it is indispensable for them to view properly what it is that really matters from these piles of reports that flow into this one single centre. Then on that basis they draw the right proposals for the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned reports. Could you please tell us what is a daily operations report? And then I'm going to put a related question. What is the form of that particular document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very fact that during 24 hours information arrives non-stop at the operations centre meant that they had to be sublimated, as it were, into a single report. We called it the daily operations report. Why daily? Because it reflects what had happened over the previous 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this report written up, or is it presented orally?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report, or rather, the daily operations report, let me use the right terminology, has to be filed in writing. That is compulsory. As such, it is filed at the operations centre in the log-book of the operations centre, and it has the status of an official document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later on we're going to see several reports of this kind. At this point may we just say to the Trial Chamber whether there was a strict form regarding this report as to the type of information that it was supposed to contain. Was it a single type of question that was supposed to be answered through these reports, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer would be that such operative duty is something that we have starting from regimental level, then it exists at brigade level, corps level, all the way up to the level of General Staff. In order to monitor information more closely, the information received from subordinates, there is an exact list of particular items.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an example so that we don't have to put a document before you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I won't get the actual order right, but what -- oh, here I go again, I'm speaking too fast. The first item had to do with the situation in the surrounding area, about the enemy, rather. The second item was the situation in our own army, and then from three onwards the items go on and on and then extraordinary events if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In these daily reports was there usually a separate item that would provide information about the situation at the border belt?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I said that border units, namely, border battalions, are within the army chain of command. Therefore, if any particular event occurred that is important as far as the Chief of General Staff is concerned, then reports would have to include that, the border units' reports, that is. However, it is there as such. However, if there weren't any events that were of particular interest, then usual developments are simply not included in reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who is the person who makes the ultimate assessment? Which information is going to be included in the official report, the report that is sent on further? Which official information is going to be contained therein?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the leader of the shift in the operations centre because on the basis of establishment and rank we thought that we had people in these positions who could tell what is more important, what is less important, and what is totally unimportant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So who is this report, this written report, the daily operations report submitted to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The daily operations report is submitted to the Chief of General Staff, the deputy Chief of General Staff, the minister of defence, and to the office of the Supreme Defence Council, or rather, the military office of the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You already said who all the recipients of the report were -- or actually, let's not repeat ourselves. But it actually contains what came in on a daily basis from the armies and from those who were the immediate subordinates of the Chief of the General Staff. In addition to these regular daily reports, were there any other reports that came in on interim basis?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Interim reports did arrive from others as well; however, before I respond to this question I believe that it is necessary for me to say by way of clarification that every day at 2100 hours the duty officers that we had in the intelligence administration and in the security administration together with the shift at the operations centre, just as we were there, they analyse the reports and they decide what is going to be placed into the daily operations report for the Chief of General Staff from all of these other reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want to lead in any way, but what you said just now, does that mean that the intelligence administration and the security administration also had their duty officers 24 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did you receive those interim reports from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, are you abandoning the other question? Are you abandoning the question that remains unanswered? You asked a question and the witness said: Before I answer, he explained something, and never got back to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is what I wanted to deal with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I wanted to ask. Yes, that's what I wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. There were other reports as well that had to do with the environment as such, and from time to time they would come from the Serb army of Krajina and Republika Srpska. They were used for writing up this report. I say "from time to time," because it wasn't a permanent practice, as it were. It really depended on what they wanted to do and on an ad hoc basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's try to be as specific as possible. You said the Serb army of the Krajina and the Republika Srpska. Did you mean the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry if I misspoke. I did misspeak, yes. From the Main Staffs of the Serb Army of Krajina and Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, as for your operations centre or the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, why was it important for them to receive reports from the Army of Republika Srpska and the Serb Army of the Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it would be lacking in seriousness if we did not express interest in what was going on in the neighbourhood, as it were. I'm trying to present this in very vivid terms, everyday terms. Any neighbour wants to know what's going on in his neighbourhood, and if there is a fire - and I'm saying a fire conditionally - you don't really want a fire to spread. And we did not want the security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to be jeopardised in any way. We wanted to take timely measures in order to prevent any security threat to the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you - and when I say you I'm referring to the operations centre of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, did you have a direct link or direct communication with the Main Staffs of the Army of Republika Srpska and the Serb Army of the Krajina? Do you know whether they had their own operations centre? Perhaps this is a compound question, but I'm sure that you can answer it.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the leave of the honourable Trial Chamber I would like to elaborate a bit on this particular question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was in existence, there was a single system of communications, communication channels, everything that comprises infrastructure. As certain republics of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia became independent, these communications were broken off but parts of that system of communications continued to function between the Republika Srpska, the Republic of the Serb Krajina, and from time to time we would use those communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpretation says "While the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was in existence ..." Are you talking about the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or are you talking about the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a slip of the tongue on my part. I meant the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which was a single state at the time. Now, as individual republics were leaving the system was disrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just tell me, in view of your previous answer, but I think it can be seen from the answer itself, do you know whether the Main Staffs of these two armies, namely, the Army of Republika Srpska and the Serb Army of the Krajina, whether they had their own operations centre that had round-the-clock duty?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in all armies of the world - and therefore in our army as well and in the Army of Republika Srpska and in the Serb Army of the Krajina - there were duty organs such as operations centres from the General Staff via corps level down to brigade level, as I explained for the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about your operative centre, did it have communication with them through the systems that were still in place from the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. You told us why it was in your interest to get that information and that you received it occasionally. Do you remember whether the VJ requested to receive this information from those armies more often with regard to that occasional character?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before General Perisic had taken over the position of Chief of General Staff, that is, at the time of General Panic, as far as I know measures were taken and requests were sent out to them to send us reports more frequent so that we might monitor the situation more closely. When Mr. Perisic became Chief of General Staff, on several occasions he sent out requests to the Main Staffs of both armies to submit reports to us in a timely fashion. But they failed to do so in spite of numerous requests to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at some documents. I selected some documents and will ask you whether you're familiar with that format of document, whether such documents arrived at your operations centre. So I will focus on the format or the shape of the document. Let us see Prosecution Exhibit P1489. I have a hard copy for you, General, if I could ask the usher to pass it on to the witness. This is a document of the Main Staff of the VRS dated 17 May 1994. I would like to hear your comments, sir, what kind of document this is and whether such documents arrived at the operations centre, and on the basis of which can you draw that conclusion if so.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document or actually a report submitted by the Main Staff of the VRS. We can see to who it was addressed. Among others it was sent to the Chief of Staff. In this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Chief of staff of which ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This, I repeat, is a document of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the Judge actually asked about the staff, which staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Chief of General Staff of the VJ. And to my mind this is a high-quality comprehensive document signed by the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic, and it was received by the General Staff of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If such a report was received by you is that something that the operations centre would consider including in their daily operational report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is directly addressed to the Chief of General Staff. It was common practice for a document addressed personally to the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ rather than to the operative centre of the General Staff was handed directly to the Chief of General Staff with the daily operations report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now look at another document. It's also a Prosecution exhibit, P901.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I have a hard copy for the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a directive for further operations, number 6, issued by the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska. It is dated 11 November 1993. General, was this document sent to you - and here I mean the operations centre of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nor to anybody in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How can you tell?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, firstly you can see that the person who drafted this directive enumerated the commands to who this was meant to go, the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the Eastern Bosnian Corps, the Herzegovina Corps, the Drina Corps, the air force, and anti-aircraft defence. So we are not mentioned at all. And secondly, if it had been sent to us, although no mention of us is to be found here, it would have been registered at the General Staff of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a serious military act. Do you remember that at any time while you were there this directive number 6 was sent to anybody in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know. And to your remark that this is a serious document, I can add that this is a document from the highest level of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could we now please see Prosecution Exhibit P903. This is a similar document at least with regard to its format as the previous one. This is a document issued by the Supreme Command of the armed forces of Republika Srpska. This is directive number 7 dated 8 March 1995. I will now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we are still on number 6. If you could just wait for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Yes, let's wait for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, the same question to you, can you tell by looking at this document that one of the recipients of this document was the VJ or any of its institutions or any personality belonging to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose that the reasons are the same as before?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it cannot be seen that one of the recipients is the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the VJ is not a recipient.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I said that it cannot be seen that it is -- can you please repeat. No, no, not necessary. The answer has been recorded. Fine. I showed you this document during the proofing. Do you remember from the time when you were in that position of yours, at that time did you hear of directive number 7 of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it when you showed it to me during the proofing. Earlier or, as it were, in real time I never saw it or heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll phrase my next question very briefly, so we don't have to go through the entire document, and I also asked you these questions during the proofing. Have you heard of Operation Spreca 95?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of some other names too, but only when you were proofing me but not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me be more precise then. When you were chief of an administration, did you hear of Operation Zvijezda 95, Star 95?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Lukavac 95?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sadejstvo 95?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us look at another document. It's from the 65 ter list of the Defence. [In English] 00424D. [Interpretation] We have a copy for you, General. And the question will be the same. Take your time to look at the document. This is a report of the Main Staff of the VRS dated 19 July 1995. Can you tell us whether this document, among others, was sent to the VJ or anybody in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document did not arrive at the General Staff of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is the document similar to the one before that you called a high-quality report? By its format does it resemble the other, the one from 1994 and which did arrive?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could we please see on the screen document P2183.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, what is the Defence's intention with --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honours. And I apologise. I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's Exhibit Number D208.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now what is the document you're asking for now, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the Defence Exhibit -- this is a Prosecution Exhibit P2183.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is an intelligence report of the intelligence affairs sector of the Main Staff of the VRS dated 25 May 1995. My question to you, Mr. Simic, is: Did this report reach anybody on the VJ, and did you receive it at the operations centre? What can you tell by the format of the document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can conclude is that this is an intelligence security report and that it was submitted to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, to the security administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, rather. If you allow me, I will elaborate a bit. This is an example showing that the security administration received -- security administration received this kind of information through its own duty centre, but the operative -- but the duty centre did not. The duty officer at the security administration assessed what would be taken from that report and put into the daily operations report for the Chief of General Staff and what the chief of the security administration will report directly to the Chief of General Staff. To put it in very simple terms, not a single sentence from this report necessarily has to be part of the daily operations report since it was sent to a different organisational unit of the General Staff, that is to say the security administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How do you determine, sir -- we only see the first page. How do you determine that it was sent to the security staff of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on page 2 it says towards the bottom the security administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. There is a stamp as to when this was received by telegram at the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 3 in English and page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. Now in your answer, sir -- I'm trying to -- in your answer at page 15 starting from line 20 you say: "If you allow me, I will elaborate a bit. This is an example showing that the security administration received -- security administration received this kind of information through its own duty centre, but the operative -- but the duty centre did not." When you say "the duty centre did not," are you talking about the duty centre of the operative centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if that is what is written there as was interpreted to me then it was not put right. I repeat once again. This information that arrived to the chief of the security administration and in the security administration there is no operations centre. There is an operations duty officer, a single person. Then that person at 2100 hours, when he comes to the operations centre to compile the daily report, he can give part of the content of this information and put it into the report but not necessarily. He consults his own chief of administration, who will decide whether he will in direct contact with the Chief of General Staff inform him about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A few moments ago you mentioned, General, that these reports of the Army of Republika Srpska and Krajina -- I think that we actually need the next page in English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait, wait, wait, before you go to the next page in English, I accept that when we got to the distribution list that the VJ would be mentioned here or the security centre of the VJ would be mentioned. I still don't see it. So my earlier question as to how he determined -- yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I can help, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe on page 4 of the English we'll find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I had wished to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, a few moments ago you mentioned that these reports from these two other armies arrived from time to time and that you - I'm speaking now about the Army of Yugoslavia - sometimes saw these reports more frequently. We're going to show another document now, P1617, it's a Prosecution exhibit. [In English] P1617. [Interpretation] This is a document of the operations administration, or rather, the operations centre of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia dated the 6th of February, 1993. I would like to ask you for a brief comment with regard to this document.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke previously I pointed out that while General Panic was still Chief of General Staff requests were sent to one or the other army for them to submit reports so that the Army of Yugoslavia could be kept abreast of how the situation developed. We see in this specific document that the assistant Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia for operations affairs was Lieutenant-Colonel -- General Zoran Stojkovic. That is to say, that even back then it was necessary to monitor the situation in the territories of these armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it's a very run-of-the-mill question, but for the transcript, if somebody has authority over somebody else in military hierarchy, does that person then make requests to the other party or issue orders?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as control and command is concerned, in our military doctrine and strategy of armed struggle it is defined who issues orders to who and where one speaks in a tone which implies a request. That tone underlying a request is used vis-à-vis those institutions that are not my subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. A small correction in view of the English translation in the document. It says "please," and I'm pleased with the word "please" used in the English translation; however, the interpreters in court are using the word "request." Could the interpreters please correct themselves. The witness said "could you please" "molimo vas" so could we have an exact interpretation of that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that "molimo vas" is "could you please."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see on our screens document [In English] 65 ter 00625D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, unfortunately we don't seem to have a hard copy of this document, so I'm going to ask for the B/C/S to be zoomed in. Yes, now I see that it's being enlarged for you, and you will be able to see this document better. Can you read it now?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the document slowly to yourself -- not aloud, no, no, just to yourself. Just to yourself. Just to yourself and then could I have a brief comment. I have a hard copy for the general now. I do apologise. This document is addressed to the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and it's signed by Blagoje Kovacevic, Major-General Blagoje Kovacevic. What can you say about this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the first sentence of this document that I have to read - and it reads as follows: "Due to lack of organisation on the part of the Main Staff of the Republic of Serb Krajina army, and the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska in providing ..." and so on and so forth. And "in order to overcome these shortcomings and improve the co-operation between us, we hereby propose ..." That is to say that the chief of the administration, General Kovacevic, due to difficulties in carrying out the orders of the Chief of General Staff hereby informs him of the problems that are there, and he proposes to him which measures should be taken because this goes beyond the powers of the chief of administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said due to difficulties in carrying out the order received from the Chief of General Staff. What was that order of the Chief of General Staff that was sent to General Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we said that from time to time they should send reports, and from the previous report when General Zoran Stojkovic is asking them to please do such and such a thing we saw that there was a problem. Now the problem continues. While Blagoje Kovacevic is the chief of administration and he is asking the Chief of General Staff the following: If he wants the administration to prepare the right kind of information for him about the situation in those areas, that he should take certain measures. I did not deem it necessary to read out all those measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Chief of General Staff agrees to that, then the administration uses this same tone presenting a request by saying "please." And only then is this sent on further, to the Main Staffs included.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please sit closer to the microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could the witness -- Madam interpreter, who do you want to sit close to the microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter was asking if the witness could come closer to the microphones, he's a bit far from the microphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have the witness please -- and try to get the microphones closer to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, page 20, line 18, the witness said -- the previous request when General Stojkovic, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He didn't say the previous request, he said a previous report.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It was request as to please do such and such a thing. That was the interpretation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, this document does not have a date. However, can you give us a tentative period of time when this document could have been reported on the basis of when General Kovacevic held that post?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was written in mid-1993, tentatively.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The previous one was written in 1993 at the time of Mr. Stojkovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Saxon, I didn't even hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe my colleague anticipated the objection that I -- that I was going to make, so I can sit down now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know at what time General Blagoje Kovacevic was chief of this sector?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blagoje Kovacevic received the position of chief of sector in November 1993 when he handed over the position of chief of first administration to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That will be Exhibit Number D209.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Before you carry on, you indicated that the operations centre was doing this in order to get information from your neighbours. Did you get similar reports as you did from the RSK and the VRS, did you get that from the Croatian army, and perhaps the Bosnian army, telling you about the situation in their respective areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we did not receive reports from them, but the situation in those areas was dealt with in the reports of these armies. That was one route, and the other was through the intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any reason you didn't ask for reports from the armies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the simple reason is that we were receiving reports from friendly armies in simple terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In even simpler terms, do I understand you to say that those armies of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina were not friendly armies to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, tell us, please, what -- what the term "team on duty" means. What's the meaning of that phrase? I started with a general question and then I will give you a document. So please explain the term.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly I should have explained previously what the Chief of General Staff relied upon to establish such teams. In the first administration of the General Staff, that is, the General Staff had a directive about special measures of permanent combat-readiness. That is a complex document which contains provisions for the Army of Yugoslavia to be brought into full combat-readiness by implementing certain measures. One of these measures was the establishment of operative duty teams. These teams were established with the intention that a larger number of more complex problems that the operations centre is faced with should be -- that it should be possible to assess them better. And based on that, that high-quality proposals be made to the Chief of Staff of the VJ so that he may take adequate measures. This will -- this can also be seen from the preamble of the order of the Chief of General Staff by which he appoints or establishes operations duty teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now look at the document. Can we see P859 on the screen, please, and for my learned friends from the Prosecution let me add that this is the very same document that -- on our 65 ter list is marked 00877. It has the status of exhibit already.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please pass a copy of this document to General Simic, please. Could we now see page 2 in both B/C/S and English. This is just a cover sheet. I'm interested in the order itself. Actually, what I would like to show is on page 3 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this is an order signed by the Chief of General Staff of the VJ, and it's dated 12 April 1994. It's about the establishment of operations duty teams. Witness, tell us who drafted this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was drafted by the first administration. I have said that the preamble reads: "Pursuant to the VJ Rules of Service item 197 and the directive on special measures of permanent combat-readiness of the VJ, chapter 1, item 1, sub-item 3, and chapter 3, items 1 and 4." And "in order to monitor the readiness of command and the creation of conditions for the constant assessment of the situation in the VJ, I hereby order ..." And it goes on to deal with the establishment of these teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the document speaks for itself, but who heads these teams in terms of the chain of command and why is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the complexity of the situation in the country and in neighbouring countries and depending on the degree of threat that arises from that situation, different variants are possible so that either the chief of administration can be the head of that team and it can go to the level of chief of sector. And the members in that case are the chiefs of administrations. This shows that it was paramount to assist the situation in a timely fashion and correctly and likewise this also applies to the -- to proposing measures. On the other hand, the Chief of Staff considered it necessary for the -- for the personnel in the General Staff not to be exhausted too much, but rather that this operative duty team be only used from time to time if there's a need to have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that this is -- that it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed. We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have to move to a private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document P861. It's a document under seal and that was the reason I asked for a private session. We also have a copy for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, a while ago we discussed the duty team, and you explained to us what it was, and we saw a document about how they were structured. Let me ask you this about this document in particular. We see that this is a report of the 26th of May, 1994, and we see here that it says "duty team." Can you tell us a few words about this document.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a duty operations officer report about the activities in the former BiH, the Army of Republika Srpska, and the Army of the Republic of Serbia and Krajina. We can see the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just correct you, please, maybe it's a mistake. It says, Report on the situation on the activities in the former B&H, VRS, and RS. There is no mention of the Serbian Republic of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that when this report was compiled, a duty team was established based on the previous order that we saw?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we have this kind of duty team functioning, does the operations centre continue to perform its regular duties?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Daily operations reports were much more complex documents. It encompasses more information, both in the territory and in the VJ. However, this particular report refers only to the situation in the former BH and the Army of Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska itself. And when this kind of report is made, a daily operations report is drafted as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is meant by the former BiH? What is it called now that it is no longer BiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we know that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a single republic incorporated into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. At this point it was actually divided between two armies and between two political leaderships. For that reason this term "former" is being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. And I want to know what -- now that it's been divided into two, what does "former" mean? Does "former" mean the two areas that have been divided put together? Does it mean Republika Srpska? Does it mean BiH minus Republika Srpska? What does it mean? Or does it mean the whole of them -- of the two of them put together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It means the entire Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its constituent parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Including Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Republika Srpska as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And -- okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In order not to try and guess, this item 4 entitled "continue to observe the signed truce, particularly in the protected areas," do you know what the provenance of this information that arrived at the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information was received from their subordinates from their operations centre, and it reached us. On that basis they have compiled these bullet points.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Their, whose?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can go back to an open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move back into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will the court officer please help us by opening the blind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now look at another document. it's Prosecution Exhibit P1017.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document comes from the Main Staff of the Serbian army of Krajina of 21st December 1993. We see who it is addressed to. Can you tell us whether this regular operations report was submitted to your operations centre or not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This specific report was not forwarded through the operations centre but was submitted to the Chief of General Staff, because the Main Staff of the Serbian army put it like that. It says: "To General Momcilo Perisic personally." And if it's not sent from the communications centre and it's sent encrypted, then it is forwarded directly to the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now have called up document of the Prosecution, and it's an entirely different subject. I have finished with this topic relating to operation centres. It's P1123. It's another document issued by the first administration, and I would kindly ask you to comment on this document in the context of the time when you were in your position. It's dated the 23rd of February, 1995. It was addressed to the Main Staff of the Serbian army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I note that the English version is dated the 23rd of March, and I can see it's the 23rd of February in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I see the difference as well, Your Honours. If that's the only discrepancy, we can just state this for the record instead of asking for a new translation. Hopefully there are no other mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is reference in this document to a letter, but I'm interested in item 1. First of all, the Chief of General Staff signed this, but can you tell me who the author was of this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first administration was the author. It was signed by the Chief of General Staff. It is addressed to the Main Staff of the Serbian army of Krajina from the very response, because it says, Reference your telegram, strictly confidential, et cetera, I presume that it was Momcilo Perisic's response to some of the requests or demands posed by the Serbian army of Krajina. Item 1 reads literally as follows: "In the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia it is not possible to organise gathering of volunteers by relying on the structures of Yugoslav Army, but rather that activities should be done through the structures outside of the Army of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that how it was in practice?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please comment item 7 of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 7 speaks about sending officers from the Yugoslav Army to the Serbian army of Krajina, and it reads that this secondment can only be regulated on the voluntary basis; which means that they requested the Chief of General Staff to force all the officers originally from that area, but he didn't agree with that and that is why he sent this kind of response.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, have you ever heard of the so-called co-ordinating meetings of the three armies, all the so-called co-ordination activities?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that I was in one of the administrations, I have heard of and I am aware of and I took part in the preparation of certain tasks and in solving certain tasks deriving from this kind of meetings and co-ordinating activities. I wasn't personally present at this co-ordinating meetings myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since you have some information about that, what can you tell the Chamber about it? What kind of meetings were those, just in few words, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, can this witness tell us what kind of meetings they were if he never attended them? Or can he tell us of the kind of tasks that he carried out that came from the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand your point. I wanted to ask him that on the basis of information he received would he be able to tell us something about the nature of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, let's start from the beginning. Who gave you tasks relating to these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Co-ordination meetings were held not on a regular basis, for instance, once a month, but as the need arose and based on the requests that came from Main Staffs of the armies. But since my head of sector was always present at these meetings he himself had to prepare based on the requests and Main Staffs the topics to be discussed at these meetings. So through my head of sector I became familiar with the tasks, but that took place in the aftermath of these meetings. And these particular requests referred to the first administration specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any specific task that the head of the sector gave you that stemmed from these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the most common requests made at these meetings was to provide assistance in literature to be provided by the first administration. Also, we were asked to provide topographic maps because the military geographical institute had the maps of the entire Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at Prosecution document P25177, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we have that number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: P2177, exhibit, prosecution. [Interpretation] I ask the usher to show this hard copy to General Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The document is self-explanatory. My question is: This was made by the first administration. Why was it important to you to know the exact disposition of the units of the SVK and the disposition of the enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For security reasons, that is, because of the security of our own country and to be able to take certain measures. But this document also shows what I have spoken about before, namely, that their reports were not submitted regularly nor were they complete. They sent them when they deemed necessary. The very beginning of the document reads: "For the next co-ordination meeting please bring..." et cetera. I believe that the rest is not so important.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, you don't have to read it out till the end. Do you know whether you requested information from the operative centre by phone when you didn't get it from them?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oftentimes I was sore at my officers and they were sore at me because we intervened through their duty officers in the operations centre, and they would simply reply, "No news, everything's fine."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to a different topic now. We have seen that one of the tasks of your administration was strategic camouflage or masking. Can you explain that notion in a few words, please?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the duties of the first administration of the General Staff was strategic masking or camouflage. In simple terms, this refers to documents - and that's the plural here - that are meant to deceive other parties about the real intentions of the VJ; or we can put it this way: We protected the commands and units of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see Prosecution -- sorry, no, not Prosecution document but our 65 ter document 01196 on the screen, please. I apologise, I didn't add the letter D at the end. So 01196D is the proper reference from the Defence list. Yes, this is it. What is this, General, can you enlighten us?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the documents of strategic masking or camouflage. If you look at it you will think that this is a missile system. Specifically, this is the Neva missile system which was used to shoot down that F-117 in 1999. But this is only a structure made of wood and sheet metal that is actually a look-alike. So this is meant by operational strategic masking or camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we assign an exhibit number to this photograph, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do that, you say this is just a look-alike. Does it work like a missile system, or it doesn't work? It's just a look-alike that doesn't work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is just a model of a missile system used to deceive the adversary about the position of the real missiles. This is not a missile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I guess the short answer is: It doesn't work like a missile.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number D210.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we'll quickly go through another document. I apologise, but I repeat 01195D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So let's follow up on Judge Moloto's question, and I'll ask you whether these are real missiles or just models?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just a model.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That which served the same purpose as the one you spoke about a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And your administration among others had this kind of responsibility too?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. We needn't repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we assign an exhibit number to this document and then we'll move on to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number D211, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, could you please tell the Court what the plan of the use of the army is.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every army, thus also the VJ, drafts a plan of its use. That plan is a complex document that elaborates how a country decided to wage war in case it's attacked. It is compiled in peacetime. The situation in the country and around it is monitored, and depending on need, it is updated. Every plan of use must contain some essential elements. There must be a directive, there must be a decision on a map, and there must be a plan of action. To elaborate the plan of use, the Chief of General Staff drafts an organisational order which regulates what must be done, who was to do it, who will know about it, the places where this is done, security measures to be applied, and finally a code-name for that plan. Once we have that, or rather, all those, the first administration together with other organisational structures as listed in the order of the Chief of General Staff starts elaborating the details of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who takes part in that process?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leading persons of the organisational units of the General Staff take part in that elaboration process with a minimum number of their subordinates or members of their organisational units. They are appointed by an order, and they must sign a special declaration that they will keep a state secret, and only then can they be involved in the elaboration of such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned three elements of the plan of use. One of these is a directive. What is a directive? What does it contain? And what is its format? Is it a document, the form of which is strictly prescribed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A directive is a highest -- the highest-level commanding document at the highest strategic level. And in our case it would be at the level of General Staff. Just like lower-level documents that stem from the directive, that is, orders of army commanders and lower-ranking commanders, it has a strictly prescribed format. So that in item 1 -- I'm now referring a strategic level directive. In item 1 it deals with the general military and political situation in the world, then it focuses in on the closer surroundings, and it presents the estimate of a certain state as to what degree it is threatened. In keeping with that estimate, the objective of the directive is subsequently stated. But first our forces are presented, et cetera. It is customary for a directive with regard to its being very general cannot be changed often. It is made for an entire war sometimes because it defines the positions of a country as to how it will wage war. That is why we do not see such directives regulating the use of the entire forces of an army often.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about a plan of action?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A plan of action is an integral part of the plan of use, as is the directive, and the plan of action lays out how the individual branches of the armed forces are to act in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How precise must the information be that is contained in the directive or the plan of action?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are at a very -- or it is at a very general level. Once excerpts are taken from such a plan of use, they are worked out in more detail so that it is precisely defined who does what, where, and when exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These extracts that you refer to, what should their form be? Who compiles them? Who are they sent to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm still speaking about the global plan of use. I have to say that it is approved by the supreme commander. The supreme commander signs the directive for use and the map decision is approved by the supreme commander. What is a map decision actually? A map decision is actually a graphic representation of what is expressed by way of text in the directive. That is why it is also approved by the president, or rather, the supreme commander, and it is signed by the chief of General Staff as the elaborating party, as it were. Now, in this hierarchy there is another link that is important though not unimportant, and that is approved by the Chief of General Staff, and it is elaborated by the assistant -- or rather, it is signed by the assistant Chief of General Staff for operations and staff affairs. That is the sequence involved in the hierarchy so that a directive would -- or rather, so that a plan of use would be valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The question that I --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, if you allow me. I don't want it to be understood that the plan of use contains only these three documents. Later on all arms and services elaborate their own attachments for the realisation of the tasks from the directive, and then once this plan of use is completed it has three or four volumes this big, and that is the plan of use.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said "this big" and you showed it with your hands and we cannot have that in the transcript. Can you tell us specifically, say how many binders like this it should contain?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, looking at your binder, perhaps it would be about ten of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We still don't have Mr. Lukic's binder on the record. Can you make sure that we have an idea what size this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us roughly how many pages? Perhaps that would be the most specific way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an exact page number because it contains maps, it contains graphs as to how units will be brought in, also calculations, and all the rest. So it's very hard for me to say anything specific in that regard. However, if you allow me to show it with my hand, it is this high, it is this many documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From the table or from the floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be best if you were to establish it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Moloto, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is tens of thousands of pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, what I asked a few moments ago, but let's be very specific. You said the word "extract," you said the word "extracts." Can you explain to us what extracts are and in what form they are compiled. Let us be specific. Who is it that compiles these extracts or writes them?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The protagonist or the proponent is the first administration, the proponent or the protagonist of the plan of use, and it involves all the organisational units of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what are extracts?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Extracts -- extracts are parts of the plan of use that pertain to certain subordinates, particular subordinates. Imagine if all of that were to be submitted to the army command, they would need ten days to study all of that and then when are they going to carry it out? So it is this group that actually elaborated the plan of use that extracts only what is essential for carrying out the task of that particular army, then the air force, the navy, because many things are important for me but are not important for others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, these armies, or rather, all the arms and services, do they work on this in depth, on this plan of use, from the lowest-ranking unit onwards?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Plans of use are elaborated in written form from regiment level upwards via brigades and artillery battalions, then corps, all the way up to the General Staff. May I also note that for a variety of reasons, primary security-related reasons, all plans are written in two copies. The first copy is always kept in a special room for safe-guarding the war plan. It is secured technically and physically. The second copy is kept in the superior command, in the same kind of room for keeping the war plan. That is for security reasons so that if for some reason the command of the brigade is destroyed, they should not be without a plan of use. It has to exist, say, in the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, have you heard of a Drina plan?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you personally take part in the elaboration of Drina plan?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have on our screens document P2125. I know that earlier on it was a protected document, but I think it is no longer so. It's a public document now. I checked that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do that, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Simic, you've told us that the first copy is always kept in a special room for safe-guarding the war plan. And then you said the second copy is kept in the superior command. Where is the first copy kept? This one is in the superior command, where is that other one, the first one kept? Or is that top secret that we are not supposed to know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The command that elaborates plans of use has a special room that is technically secure, and there is always a guard in front of the door. And there is an opening there so he can see inside the safe boxes where the plan is kept. The second copy is submitted to the superior command, that safe-guards it along with their own plan in that same kind of room or one perhaps that is even bigger depending on the capacity of the rooms involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document Prosecution Exhibit P215, P215, page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 215 what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I have a copy of the document for you. The first thing I'm going to ask you pertains to this very first page. It has a stamp showing that it was locked in your administration on the 14th of November, 1993. Sorry that I've been leading.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us about this? Do you know this document, and what was it that you did in relation to this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am fully familiar with this document because I was one of the participants in the elaboration of this document. It shows what I spoke about in terms of directives in general, the military/political situation, what is going on and where. Then there is a reference to possible threats, that is point 2, aggression against Serb lands. Then there are the objectives of the aggression, then there is an explanation of how this aggression would probably take place, then how the forces taking part in the aggression could be supported. And then finally on page 6, Roman numeral II, there is a reference to our own forces, general objective, what the state actually wants, then the concept of activities in general, how that is envisaged to be implemented within this general objective. On page 8, Roman numeral III, there is a reference to the tasks of the armed forces of the Army of Yugoslavia, the Army of Republika Srpska, the Serb Army of the Krajina, then the use of RV, that is to say the air force and air defence, and then -- then there are other aspects such as the moral, political, logistics support for combat activities, and so on. That is to say that this is a complex directive, as you can see on the basis of what I've been saying, and it is one of the key parts of the plan of use. This directive is used for the map decision and for the action plan. They operationalise what is defined in its text.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There are some attachments there as well, but the document is self-explanatory so we really don't have to refer to them right now, I mean, after the directive itself, there are these attachments. You said that you took part in the elaboration of this directive. It says here November 1993. Does that perhaps jog your memory? Did you work on this document roughly at that time, as is written on this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to yourself, do you remember who else worked on this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that from the General Staff the top people of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia were involved. So I don't have to enumerate them all by name specifically because I cannot remember exactly who held which position then. I know that in addition to officers of the Army of Yugoslavia there were other active participants in the elaboration of this directive, namely, General Manojlo Milovanovic from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and General Mile Novakovic, also from the Main Staff of the Serb Army of Krajina. Along with them there were a few officers whom they had brought along in order to facilitate the elaboration of the document. The directive was signed by the president of the Supreme Defence Council, Zoran Lilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us just comment upon a few parts of the directive itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have page 3 in B/C/S and page 3 in English concerning item 2 Entitled "Aggression against Serb lands."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read it out and ask for your comment. "The general objective of the aggression is to break up the FRY, prevent the creation of a single Serb state in the Balkans, and ensure the relocation of NATO forces from CEV to JEV." What does that mean, CEV and JEV?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And ensure the relocation of NATO forces from the central European front to the south-east -- south European front.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With the objective of acquiring full control of the sources of raw materials in Asia and Africa and control of developments in the former USSR. (A), Croatia's objective is to establish authority within its administrative borders; (B), the Muslims' objective continues to the creation of a unified Muslim state in the territory of the former BH with access to the sea, the Drina river, and the Sava river, and the objective of the Croatia Republic of Herceg-Bosna continues ..." I don't want to read the whole text. On the basis of which information is this entered into the directive?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This comes from intelligence on the basis of intelligence gathered, knowledge acquired in the immediate area over a longer period of time, the intelligence people came to the conclusion that a possible aggression could evolve in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next page, please, page 4 both in B/C/S and in English. We see that the document is from November 1993. Now I'm going to read (A) "probable mode of action of the Croatian army," and it says: "The aggression would start with an all-out attack of the Croatian army on the Republic of the Serb Krajina with a radical objective. In the beginning they would engage their main forces in Western Slavonia and Baranja with the objective to simultaneously draw Republika Srpska and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia into the war and condemn them before the international public and ask for help from the organisation of the United Nations, with a view to protection." Who enters this information into the directive, on the basis of what?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An intelligence man, but let us be clear about this. This is not the fruit of the work of one person, but rather all the personnel of the General Staff who estimated or made estimates about the objectives of the aggression based on the development of the situation in the immediate vicinity up to that time and based on orders received from the leadership. But basically it's the intelligence people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, do you know about the events termed Operation Flash? Have you heard about it, and can you say in a few words what happened in that operation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have already read out some of that in the previous text and it was quite implemented in May 1995 in Operation Flash when the Croatian army attacked Western Slavonia, evicted the population, and occupied those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at page 7 in the B/C/S and page 8 in the English. We're now referring to that part of the directive that is called, "The Use of the Armed Forces." I'm interested in the part referring to the VJ. It's under item 2. It's probably the previous page in the English where it starts, that is the bottom of the previous page. About the Army of Yugoslavia, it says: "Repel the potential aggressors by combat-readiness of the Army of Yugoslavia, prevent potential aggressors, and prevent armed rebellion ..." and it continues on the following page, "and thus make the leadership of the Republic of Croatia and the former BiH to accept the situation in the theatre of war."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I couldn't follow because I couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's -- the page reference is 6 in B/C/S and then toward the -- in the centre part of this paragraph. I skipped the part referring to the RS and the RSK, and it starts --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I've found it, combat-readiness of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, do explain to us what that means, combat-readiness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, very sorry to interrupt. Mr. Harmon and I are -- have lost the plot. If you could specific which page we are in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Welcome to the club.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, well, I didn't want to read. What the page reference is in the English is page 7 and page 8. It starts at the bottom of page 7. Let's see whether that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where do we find combat-readiness on that page?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's been suggested by Mr. Harmon that there are small or slight differences between the interpretation, the live interpretation, and the translation as we can see it in the document.
